payload.name: resonant-peak
payload.scope: To quantify the maximum amplification in a closed-loop system's frequency response, so designers can assess relative stability and predict time-domain ringing.

definition.body: Resonant-peak is a human-made stability measure that quantifies the maximum magnitude of a closed-loop system's frequency response, occurring at the resonant frequency where the amplification is greatest. Parameters: (1) the closed-loop transfer function T(jw) = G(jw)/(1 + G(jw)H(jw)); (2) the resonant frequency wr where the magnitude of T(jw) achieves its maximum; (3) the peak magnitude Mr = max of the magnitude of T(jw) over all frequencies. For a standard second-order underdamped system, Mr = 1/(2*zeta*sqrt(1-zeta^2)) and wr = wn*sqrt(1-2*zeta^2), where zeta is the damping ratio, providing a direct quantitative link between frequency-domain amplification and time-domain transient quality. It is distinct from bandwidth (the frequency span where the gain exceeds -3 dB, not the maximum gain), gain-margin (the gain headroom at the -180 degree phase crossing, a different stability measure), and peak-overshoot (the time-domain exceedance of the steady-state value, not the frequency-domain amplification). Persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard relative-stability specification in classical control engineering - measured from the Bode magnitude curve of closed-loop frequency responses, computed from analytical transfer functions, and specified in design requirements for servo systems, filter design, and vibration control - encoded in control textbooks (Ogata's Modern Control Engineering; Franklin, Powell, and Workman's Digital Control of Dynamic Systems), simulation tools, and aerospace control design practice. e.g.: the resonant peak Mr = 1.15 of a second-order system with zeta=0.5, attained at wr = 0.71wn; the closed-loop peak of a second-order low-pass filter with zeta=0.4 read from the Bode magnitude curve as Mr = 1.36; the design guideline bounding Mr below 1.5 to limit step overshoot, per Ogata's Modern Control Engineering | not: bandwidth (the passband width, not the peak gain); gain-margin (the gain headroom at the -180 degree phase crossing, not the peak magnitude); peak-overshoot (the time-domain exceedance, not the frequency-domain amplification) [formal: culminans amplificatio | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]
